title: Microscopic Theory of Drag in a Bose Condensate Interacting with a Moving Reservoir
authors: Hassan Alnatah, Shuang Liang, Shouvik Mukherjee, Qi Yao, Ashton S. Bradley, David W. Snoke
abstract: We derive a microscopic theory of drag for a Bose-Einstein condensate interacting with a moving reservoir. Starting from interactions between a condensate and a drifting fermionic bath, we integrate out the bath degrees of freedom within the Born--Markov approximation to obtain an effective Gross--Pitaevskii equation with a drag potential. From this potential we derive an effective drag force and obtain a closed expression for the drag coefficient, determined by the reservoir density fluctuations and the condensate density profile. As an application, we simulate the drag for an exciton--polariton condensate interacting with a drifting electron gas.
summary: This paper develops a microscopic theory for calculating the drag force on a Bose-Einstein condensate due to interaction with a moving fermionic reservoir. By employing the Born-Markov approximation, the authors derive an effective drag potential that modifies the condensate's Gross-Pitaevskii equation. The resulting drag force is shown to be linearly proportional to the relative velocity, providing a fundamental understanding of dissipation in quantum fluids.
main_problem: The paper derives a microscopic theory to calculate the drag force experienced by a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) when it interacts with a moving, noncondensed fermionic reservoir.
main_result: The drag force is found to be proportional to the relative velocity between the condensate and the reservoir, leading to a friction law $F = -\Gamma_d (v_\psi - v_d)$.
method: The derivation uses the Born-Markov approximation to eliminate reservoir degrees of freedom, resulting in an effective, history-dependent drag potential added to the Gross-Pitaevskii equation.
model_or_system: The system consists of a BEC (bosons, $\psi$) interacting with a drifting fermionic bath (reservoir, $\phi$). The interaction is modeled via a Hamiltonian, and the dynamics are governed by an effective G-P equation incorporating the drag potential.
key_observables: Drag potential ($V_{	ext{drag}}$), drag force ($F$), and the friction coefficient ($\Gamma_d$).
important_parameters: Reservoir density fluctuations, condensate density profile, and the relative drift velocity ($v_\psi - v_d$).
main_assumptions: The Born approximation, the Markov approximation (short reservoir memory), and the assumption that the reservoir is spatially uniform and in a steady state.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the condensate interacting with a drifting reservoir, leading to a drag potential, and shows how the momentum distribution shifts based on the relative drift velocity.
paper_structure: The paper builds the theory by starting from the full Hamiltonian, applying approximations to derive the master equation, transforming it into the Schrödinger picture, and finally deriving the explicit form of the drag potential and the resulting force equation.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, microscopic derivation of dissipation (drag) in quantum gases, connecting the environment's fluctuations (via the Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation) directly to the macroscopic dynamics of the condensate.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic of a condensate interacting with a moving reservoir. (a) A condensate ψ interacting with a reservoir drifting with a velocity vd, producing a drag potential Vdrag acting on the condensate. (b) Momentum distribution N(k) of the moving condensate: the reservoir current accelerates it (co-drift) or slows it toward k = 0 (counter-drift), relative to no drift.

Figure 2. Schematic of the simulated polaritons in a one- dimensional wire. A non-resonant pump laser shown in red is focused near one end of the wire generating a polariton condensate at the pump spot and propagating ballistically along the wire (orange). A voltage bias is applied between the contacts driving a current of electrons through the wire; depending on the sign of the voltage, the electron drift velocity ±vd can be positive or negative, so that the electron flow can be made either co-propagating or counter-propagating with the condensate. The condensate flow direction defines the positive x (equivalently +k) axis.

Figure 3. Momentum-space drag of the polariton conden- sate. (a) Measured PL intensity vs. in-plane momentum k (reproduced from Ref. [3]) at 0 V (v = 0), +14 V (+115.4 µA, co-moving), and −14 V (−143.4 µA, counter- moving). (b) Simulated momentum distribution N(k) from the driven–dissipative Gross–Pitaevskii equation with the mi- croscopic drag potential, same three cases (vd = 0, ±0.14 µm/ps). In both, the forward peak shifts with the electron current (co →higher k, counter →lower k).
